# The Modular GTM Team: Specialist Depth Without a Full-Service Agency

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-modular-gtm-team/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-04 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: AI and Web3 companies often need specialist depth for short periods without carrying every specialist on payroll. A modular GTM team keeps a small senior core accountable for the commercial problem and brings in focused support when the bottleneck changes. Large advertisers already work this way, keeping most work in-house and buying agencies for capacity and specialist skill. The model works only if one team stays accountable for the outcome.

AI and Web3 companies often need strong specialists for specific periods, without needing every specialist on payroll. A modular GTM team keeps a small group accountable for the strategy and brings in focused support when the work requires it. The pattern is not new at the top of the market: in the ANA's 2023 survey, large advertisers' in-house teams handled an average of 61% of company work, and the work that went outside went mainly for capacity or specialist skills. What makes the model work is not the roster. It is one team that stays accountable for the outcome.

*AI and Web3 companies often need specialist depth without needing a large permanent team. That gap is becoming an operating model of its own.*

## Why the usual staffing options fall short

The traditional agency model is built around handing a broad problem to one outside team and expecting an integrated answer.

The freelancer model works the other way. Bring in specialists as needed and manage the system internally.

A lot of AI and Web3 companies fit awkwardly into both.

The mix of work can be unusually broad. A company may need technical positioning, founder content, ecosystem marketing, business development, partnerships, paid distribution, creative, community, events, research, automation, and regional expertise, all sometimes within the same quarter. At the same time, there may not be enough steady volume in any one area to justify building a full in-house function.

So the first problem is often organisational, not tactical.

A large full-service agency can give a company breadth, but breadth alone does not guarantee that the people doing the work are close enough to the commercial problem. The familiar failure mode is that senior people sell the engagement, execution gets split across teams, and the client ends up reconnecting strategy, media, creative, and sales themselves.

A collection of freelancers can produce the opposite problem. The specialists may be excellent, but the company becomes the project manager and integration layer. Someone still has to brief everyone, resolve conflicting recommendations, maintain context, set priorities, manage dependencies, and make the final call. Context is the expensive part. Panopto's 2018 survey of 1,000 workers estimated that 42% of institutional knowledge is unique to the individual in the role. Spread that across six freelancers with no shared record and most of the reasoning lives in other people's heads.

|  | Full-service agency | Freelancer roster | Modular GTM team |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Who owns the commercial problem | The agency, at a distance | The company, by default | A named senior core |
| Who integrates the work | Split across agency teams | The client | The core |
| Strength | Breadth, scale, procurement fit | Specialist quality, low overhead | Specialist depth with one strategy |
| Typical failure | Senior people sell, juniors deliver | Company becomes project manager | Becomes a roster if ownership slips |
| Best fit | Stable needs across many channels, large budget | One defined function with repeatable volume | Market and message still being worked out |

## The senior core keeps the commercial context

The modular GTM model is a practical middle ground.

A small senior core stays close to the business and owns the commercial problem: who the customer is, what the product needs to communicate, what the immediate objective is, which channels matter, how success will be measured, and what should happen next.

Specialists then plug in where there is a real need. That might mean programmatic media, creative, PR, development, automation, data, creator programmes, ecosystem research, events, regional execution, or a very specific technical skill.

The model only works if accountability stays clear.

Without someone owning the whole picture, a modular team is just a nicer name for a freelancer roster.

In practice that ownership needs artefacts, not just a person. The core keeps the shared brief, the definitions of what counts as a result, the record of decisions and the handoffs between specialists. Our piece on [the commercial system](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-system-what-it-is/) sets out the shared definitions and records that let several contributors work to one plan.

> Without someone owning the whole picture, a modular team is just a nicer name for a freelancer roster.

## Bring in specialist capacity when the problem changes

That ownership matters especially in markets where the bottleneck changes quickly. One month the issue is positioning. The next is distribution. Then the company needs strategic partners, a launch, a stronger content engine, or a more qualified pipeline. Building a fixed team around every temporary need gets expensive fast.

A modular structure lets the execution layer change without forcing the company to reinvent the commercial strategy every time a new specialist gets involved.

| Quarter's bottleneck | What the core keeps | Specialist brought in | Leaves when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Positioning | Customer, message, measure | Technical writer or researcher | The message is tested and written down |
| Distribution | Channel plan and budget | Programmatic or creator specialist | The channel reads, or is ruled out |
| Partnerships | Target list and terms | Ecosystem or BD specialist | Agreements are signed and owned in-house |
| Launch | Timeline and success test | PR, events, regional execution | The launch report is written |

The table is illustrative, but the logic is the one large advertisers describe. The ANA's 2023 survey of 162 members found 65% had moved established work from outside agencies to in-house over the previous three years, while 92% still used external agencies. The reasons for going outside were capacity, when the in-house team was too busy, and specialised capabilities the company lacked. The difference for a smaller company is that its core is a few senior people rather than a department.

## When this model actually fits

This is by no means an argument that full-service agencies are obsolete. They are not. Large agencies make sense when a company needs scale, standardised execution, geographic reach, procurement compatibility, or substantial production capacity.

The more useful question is which operating model matches the actual bottleneck.

If the need is one well-defined function with repeatable volume, hire or retain a specialist. If the company has stable needs across many channels and enough budget to support a large integrated account team, a traditional agency may be the right answer. But when the market, message, and commercial motion are still being worked out, a senior-led modular team can be more efficient and easier to adapt.

The labour market is moving the same way. Lightcast, a labour-market analytics firm, found at least 34,000 US workers had "fractional" in their job title in 2025, up 265% from 2019, and that 97% of US fractional postings in 2026 came from small and medium-sized companies. Part-time senior leaders are one common way a smaller company fills its core. Our guide to [agencies, consultancies, advisors and fractional executives](https://lowob.com/research/agency-vs-consultancy-vs-advisor/) sets out what each sells.

## AI raises the value of the core

AI is pushing this further. Research, first drafts, workflow automation, analysis, prototyping, and creative iteration are all becoming faster and cheaper. That does not remove the need for specialists. It means a smaller senior team can coordinate more work, while context and judgment become even more important.

Buyers report the same shift. Gartner's 2025 survey of 402 marketing leaders found 22% said generative AI had reduced their reliance on external agencies for creativity and strategy, and 39% planned to cut agency budgets. Cheaper production moves the scarce resource from output to direction.

Media works much the same way. A company may not need a permanent in-house expert for every buying platform, publisher relationship, creator network, region, or campaign type. It does need access to the right operator when the opportunity is real, with one strategy connecting the work.

That is the value of the modular model: specialist depth without carrying the organisational weight all the time. Our capstone on [building the commercial system at 20, 50 and 200 people](https://lowob.com/research/building-the-commercial-system-at-every-size/) shows how the core changes as the company grows.

Keep the commercial thinking close to the business. Bring in specialists when the problem calls for them. Keep one team accountable for the outcome.

For AI and Web3 companies still figuring out exactly how they win, that flexibility can matter more than having every capability permanently on the org chart.

## lowob takeaways

- **Name the owner.** Keep the commercial problem and outcomes with a named senior core.
- **Buy specialists for gaps.** Bring them in for a defined bottleneck rather than duplicating a full-time organisation.
- **Keep the artefacts central.** Shared briefs, definitions, decisions and handoffs stop a modular team becoming a roster.
- **Change the layer, not the strategy.** Specialists rotate as the bottleneck moves; the plan stays with the core.

## Common questions

### What is a modular GTM team?

A go-to-market model in which a small senior core owns the commercial problem, including the customer, message, objective and measure, and brings in specialists for defined gaps such as media, PR, creative or partnerships.

### Is a modular team better than a full-service agency?

It depends on the bottleneck. Full-service agencies suit stable needs across many channels with a large budget. A modular team suits companies whose market, message and commercial motion are still being worked out.

### How is a modular team different from hiring freelancers?

With a freelancer roster the company is the integrator. In a modular team a senior core owns the brief, the priorities, the handoffs and the final call, so specialists work to one strategy.

### Do large companies use specialists instead of one agency?

Many combine in-house teams with outside specialists. The ANA's 2023 survey found 82% of members had an in-house agency and 92% still used external agencies, mainly for capacity and specialist skills.
